articles.headline: Our Black Hills Trip.
articles.text:
There are so many points of interest in the Black Hills that it seems we have entered upon a hopeless task in attempting to describe them all. Before we finish, however, we must speak of Bear Gulch's tin and gold mines.

Bear Gulch proper is almost west of Spearfish and almost touching the Wyoming line. It is about 5,000 feet higher than Spearfish, and the road is as far from being a boulevard as anything we can imagine. Granite and quartz formations are constantly cropping out in the road-bed., making it very rough. There is a constant ascent all the way, except an equally as bad descent on the opposite slope of the hills. All the way there is a dense forest of lofty pines, which furnished a delightfully cool shade. We pass Potato and Beaver creek camps, noted as the scenes of successful sluice mining, and finally arrive at Bear Gulch camp and the Nigger Hill mining property. Here we stopped for dinner, and were hospitably entertained by Mr. St. John. The leaders of our party, Messrs. Johnston and Grassfield, of Spearfish, were old miners here and were thoroughly competent to show us all the points of interest.

The best and most property belongs to the Nigger Hill mining company, and but for the difficulty and expense of shipping in machinery, would vie with the Homestake system in its bi-weekly output. At present the mines are unworked. Sand creek, just over the Wyoming line, may be seen from the summit of Nigger Hill, and has also furnished profitable sluice mining. One of the largest nuggets taken from Sand creek weighs about $300, and is now owned by Mrs. Chapman. The ledges of gold ore here present about the same external appearance as those of the Homestake system, and our description will be confined mainly to the tin mines recently discovered here.

These mines were discovered by accident, through sluice-mining. Everyone has heard of the notorious black sand, the curse of sluicers. It is a very coarse sand, or fine gravel, of great specific gravity, and would be caught by the riffles in the sluice boxes as readily as gold dust. This occasioned much difficulty to the miners, both in panning and retorting, and has probably caused more dubious language than any other one obstacle. No one knew or seemed to care what was the composition of this black sand until some genius had it analyzed, and the mining world was electrified by the discovery that it was about 80 per cent. pure tin. The discovery of tin ore running from 3 to 30 per cent. followed immediately upon this, the discovery creating intense excitement.

The value of this find can best be determined by analogy. All, or virtually all, the tin in the world now comes from the Cornwall mines in England. At present these mines are [being operated?] at great depth and three miles out under the English channel. The expense of mining is consequently very large. The ore in the Cornwall mines runs from ⅓ to 1 per cent., and gigantic fortunes have been made in these mines. They have at present a monopoly of the tin trade of the world.

A glance at the difference between the Cornwall and Bear Gulch mines will show how vastly superior are the latter. In Bear Gulch the ore crops out on the surface, and there are mountains of it. It is easily mined and reduced, the only difficulty, as hitherto mentioned, being that the roads are poor, making transportation high. This difficulty is far more than counterbalanced, however, by the high grade of the Bear Gulch ore in comparison with that of Cornwall. There is none here that assays less than 3 per cent., and from this up to 30 per cent. That these mines will soon be developed is beyond all question. Here is one of the best openings for capital that can be found in the United States.

All the claims have now been located, and we found Mr. Chapman busily at work on one. An assay of his dump averaged 6 per cent. tin, and much of it runs enough gold to pay all cost of reduction, leaving the tin clear profit. Mr. Chapman has several claims, and showed us over all of them. On one is a deep shaft, which we descended, and at the bottom found a large snow drift. Immediately the snow-balls began flying at short range, and it was a sport whose novelty we fully enjoyed. Standing in a temperature of 30 degrees we could easily throw snow-balls at some of the party sweltering under a July sun at a temperature of 115 degrees. Mr. Chapman took us to his different claims and finally to his house, where his wife displayed the $300 nugget to our wondering eyes. Mr. Chapman is a good mineralogist, and has all the appliances for assaying his own ore. He has had his experiments confirmed by other assayers, and there is no doubt of the genuineness of the tin find and that at no distant day the United States will draw its supply of tin from the Black Hills instead of Cornwall.

(To be continued.)
articles.summary: Packard's continuing Black Hills travel letter describes a visit to the Bear Gulch tin and gold mines near Spearfish, guided by Johnston and Grassfield, including Mr. Chapman's claims and a snowball fight at the bottom of a shaft.

articles.text: Only a few weeks remain ere the legislative convention of this district will have placed its candidates in nomination. The citizens of Billings county may indeed be proud of having decided upon such a man as L. N. Cary as their standard bearer. Unassuming, yet thoroughly in sympathy with the needs of our people, he will make a record for himself such as few others would achieve. And to elect Mr. Cary means not only to place the right man in the right place but a victory of common sense over political intrigue and wire-pulling. Mr. Cary is in no sense a politician, in the ordinary acceptance of the word, and never sought any office. Let the people send him where he will do the most good--to the halls of the legislature.
articles.summary: Editorial urging the election of L. N. Cary, Billings county's choice, to the territorial legislature.

articles.text: Since July 18 over 250 carloads of fat cattle from Colorado ranges have been shipped into Chicago over the Burlington and Quincy road.
articles.summary: Colorado range cattle shipments to Chicago since July 18.

articles.text: The wool growers of Texas are petitioning the legislature to require the railroads of that state to act with justice towards the shipment of mutton interests.--[Breeder's Gazette.
articles.summary: Texas wool growers petition for fair railroad treatment.

articles.text: The Albany Land and Cattle Company, with a capital of $5,000,000, has just been incorporated at Laramie City. The stock of the company is understood to be largely taken in Europe.--[Col. Live Stock Record.
articles.summary: Albany Land and Cattle Company incorporated at Laramie City.

articles.text: It is said that Big Timber station will ship 400,000 pounds of wool this year. Twenty-five carloads have already been shipped and as much more is to come. The wool is grown on the Sweet Grass, Big Timber and Musselshell pastures.--[Livingston Enterprise.
articles.summary: Big Timber, Montana, wool shipments.

articles.text: The demand for well-bred American young cattle was never so good as right now. A moderate bunch of yearling and two-year-old heifers were sold here on Tuesday for $30 and $33 per head. Mr. George Brockway was the purchaser.--[Denver (Col.) L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Strong demand for young cattle at Denver.

articles.text: A cowboy, whose name we forget, tells us that a rattlesnake bite has little or no effect upon a horse. All that is necessary is to open the wound and rub in a little ammonia, or in the absence of ammonia plenty of common salt, and the poison will be neutralizd.--[Exchange.
articles.summary: Remedy for rattlesnake bite in horses.

articles.text: Fifty head of grade Galloway four-year-old steers, raised by Jim Galloway, in the Paradox valley, in Montrose--animals that never ate grain or known a shelter--turn the scale beam at twelve hundred pounds each, and there is not a horn on their heads or white hair on their bodies.--[Col. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Grade Galloway steers raised in Colorado's Paradox valley.

articles.text: The governors of Wyoming, New Mexico and Montana have issued proclamations declaring a quarantine against cattle shipments from localities suspected to be infected with the cattle fever. The various railroad companies have agreed to co-operate with the state and territorial authorities in their efforts to arrest the spread of the disease.
articles.summary: Western territorial governors quarantine against cattle fever.

articles.text: The Northern Pacific cut down carload cattle rates a week or two ago, 5 per cent., to correspond with a like reduction made by the Union Pacific. On Friday, President Harris of the Northern Pacific and President Adams of the Union Pacific, met in Chicago, and after a conference agreed to restore the old rates, to take effect at once.--[Livingston Enterprise.
articles.summary: Northern Pacific and Union Pacific restore old cattle carload rates.

articles.text: In the cities of Canada the price of mutton is always as high as that of beef. This because they grow a finer sheep over in the Dominion than we do in the western States. Their big Cotswolds and their Shropshire sheep are equal to the best of Europe. There is a vast difference between the flavor of the mutton obtained at Quebec and that of Chicago.--[Colo. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Canadian mutton prices and sheep quality.

articles.text: Sheepmen of Tom Green county, Texas, in a general convention, have demanded the restoration of the wool tariff of 1867. Tom Green is the largest wool-producing county in the world, having an area of over twelve thousand square miles. Drought now prevails over the entire county, and all small streams have disappeared. Already thousands of sheep are reported to have perished.--[Kansas City L. S. Indicator.
articles.summary: Tom Green county, Texas, sheepmen and drought.

articles.text: Men who are predicting that the price of stock cattle will continue to decline will find themselves mistaken. So long as there are millions of money in Europe and America that seeks investment in live stock the price will keep up. Investment in cattle under any and all circumstances is better than investment in railroad stocks.--[Col. L. S. Record.
articles.summary: Cattle prices expected to hold up on investment demand.

articles.text: At Raton last week an intoxicated cowboy shot one J. R. Smith in the knee, inflicting a serious wound and making amputation necessary. There was no quarrel. Again we say, the six-shooter must go. Our editorial correspondent writes us from Puerto de Luna the particulars of a shooting at Chisum's ranch. In this case the killer was justified, but the fact of the killing remains the same.--[N. M. Stock Grower.
articles.summary: Shootings at Raton and Chisum's ranch, New Mexico.

articles.text: The Chicago cattle market has been struck with a serious decline in prices. A drop of $1 per hundred pounds in the best range fed beef was experienced within twenty-four hours and in prices of the same shipment. Though the market rallied slightly thereafter it has not nearly regained the standard of the past twelve months, and the feeling among dealers is that its buoyancy is gone, not to return this season. This will have an important bearing on times in that it will have a tendency to hold many cattle from the market that would otherwise be converted into cash.--[Livingston Enterprise.
articles.summary: Decline in Chicago range-beef prices.

articles.text: Another disease has made its appearance among cattle in Iowa which promises to become very serious. It attacks the eyes of stock of all ages, which first become watery, then rapidly inflame, and a white film spreads over the eye until the animal is totally blind. Stockmen say they have never seen anything like it, and the doctors are at a loss to know what to do for it. All medicines thus far tried have had no effect. Over fifty cattle in one herd are already affected, and the disease is pronounced contagious. Great alarm is felt among owners of stock in that vicinity.
articles.summary: Blinding eye disease among Iowa cattle.

articles.text: Western range cattle shippers often do well by trying new commission men, but it has been the experience of some that if "split shipments" are to be made they should be made on alternate days. A large bunch of cattle cannot often be handled to as good advantage to owners when divided into two or more lots on the same day, as when handled in one lot, and as a rule the best way to test the relative merits of salesmen on that class of cattle is to try them on different days and make proper allowances for market fluctuations. This, of course, does not apply to native cattle, hogs and sheep.--[Drovers' Journal.
articles.summary: Advice on split shipments of range cattle.

articles.text: Hugh O'Kane, who arrived from Poplar Tuesday, informs us that seven men came down the Missouri river in three boats last week, and while passing Poplar Creek they were stopped by Joe Culbertson and a party of soldiers and Indians. Five of the seven were captured and put in the [guard house?]. The other two escaped and secreted themselves in the brush which skirts the shore. They are supposed to be Pat Rolles and "Dutch." There is a reward of $1500 offered for the capture of "Dutch," who killed Cherokee's partner on the Musselshell two years ago. A large force of soldiers and Indians surrounded the brush which is about a quarter of a mile square.--[Glendive Independent.
articles.summary: Suspected outlaws captured on the Missouri near Poplar Creek, Montana.

articles.text: It is said that Texas fever has appeared among some range cattle near Spearfish, D. T., having been introduced by cattle received by rail from Texas at Ogallala, and afterward driven to Spearfish. The distance from Ogallala to Spearfish is 300 miles, which seems to demonstrate conclusively that it is necessary to trail Texas cattle for a great distance before the fever germ can be completely eliminated from their systems. The impression held by some prominent stockmen that Texas fever cannot be introduced by cattle trailed from Texas, as their nature is radically changed by the long drive, is not confirmed by this intelligence. Another blow seems to be struck, however, at the transportation of cattle from Texas by rail.--[Kansas City L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Texas fever reported among range cattle near Spearfish, D. T.

articles.text: Advices from Cottonwood, Meagher county, give a meagre account of the killing of another batch of horse-thieves on the Musselshell, some 40 miles from the town above named. A band of cowboys who were in pursuit of stolen horses discovered a cabin in the timber on a mountain side, and the fact of its being so situated and in an otherwise uninhabited region, their suspicions were at once aroused. They secreted themselves and kept watch. During the day and night small parties of men, in every case having horses in their possession, came and went. It becoming evident that the place was a horse-thief rendezvous, the cowboys set about wiping it off the face of the earth. Waiting till after night, they crept up close to the house and commenced firing on it. What the result would have been if the thieves had stood their ground it is hard to say, but the whole outfit, fourteen in number, rushed out of the house and tried to escape. Nine were shot down and killed outright, while five got away. The cowboys then set fire to the cabin and left. Although this occurred somewhere in the vicinity where Granville Stewart's cowboys were reported to have a band of thieves corralled a few days ago, we are assured that it is an entirely different affair. It seems fair to assume that Montana horse-thieves will some of these days get tired of this kind of business and reform.--[Helena Independent.
articles.summary: Cowboys kill nine horse-thieves on the Musselshell, Montana.

articles.text: As soon as Capt. Wrenshaw returns from the scene of the washout he will order a number of improvements in the freight house. The west end will be partitioned off into three rooms, and a platform will be built on the same end. A large derrick will also be erected to move heavy freight and movable skids built on which to run freight into the warehouse.
articles.summary: Planned improvements to the Medora freight house.

articles.headline: Medora Stage and Forwarding Co.
articles.text:
Much work has been done since our last issue, and of a decisive kind. Exclusive passenger and express rates have been made to Medora, and there will be no such uncertainty as there has been in the freight business. Messrs. Fee and Footner especially have been very obliging, and they willingly signed the contracts giving Medora exclusive control of the business of their departments.

Word has ceen received from Messrs. Barr and Deffebach that all the coaches and a number of the horses have been bought at Helena, and by the time this article reaches the eye of the public it is probable that all the stock will have been purchased. There is a large amount of preliminary work that takes considerable time, but much progress has been made and our readers may rest assured that every effort will be made to hasten matters. Messrs. Deffebach and Barr are expected back on almost every train with the stock, which will at once be strung along the line. Four stations have now been built and hay put up near these and several others. Wells have been dug and a number of springs close to the stations found. The boulders are being cleared from the trail on Rocky ridge, and the road-bed graded in many places.

As before announced, A. T. Packard will be general manager, Rassie Deffebach superintendent of stages, and J. C. Fisher will be local manager.
articles.summary: Progress report on the Medora Stage and Forwarding Co.'s Medora-Deadwood line: rail contracts, coaches bought at Helena, stations, wells and road work.

articles.headline: The Storm.
articles.text:
One of the most severe rain, wind and hail storms within the memory of the traditional "oldest inhabitant" visited Medora on the afternoon of August 18. The storm made up about five miles northwest of the town. When first noticed the cloud resembled an old-fashioned thunder shower, but rapidly assumed alarming proportions and took on a greenish tinge which betokened the presence of wind and hail. In about 30 minutes after the cloud was first noticed the rain began to fall, and before any movement could be made for protection the storm burst forth in all its fury. The rain fall was simply enormous, resembling more than anything else the bursting of a water-spout. The force of the wind was terriffic, taking the water up which had deluged the earth and tossed it about in all directions. The hail was very severe, some houses having every pane of of glass in the south windows broken. We have not as yet learned of any loss of life as the result of the storm. The billiard hall was put to a very severe test as to its ability to resist the force of the wind. It is quite high and narrow and almost wholly unprotected from a wind coming from the northwest. The building on the north side of the track known as "Cowboy saloon," but now unoccupied, was turned completely around, occasioning much consternation on the part of two gentlemen who had been out gathering wild plums (or oats), and returning after the storm saw the building facing differently than when they went out, came to the conclusion that they had lost their way, and, animated by the true hunter's instinct, they immediately went into camp. George still thinks there was something wrong about it.

The washouts on the railroad exceed anything known in the history of the road. Five bridges between Medora and Glendive were washed away and more than twenty-five miles of track badly damaged. Telegraph poles were strewn around promiscuously, cutting off all communication from the west. Monday's westbound passenger train was obliged to lay here three days before the damages were repaired.

The storm was about seven miles wide and forty-five miles in length. Beyond a few minor stampedes [but?] very little damage was done to stock.
articles.summary: Account of the severe rain, wind and hail storm of August 18 at Medora, which broke windows, turned the vacant Cowboy saloon around and washed out five railroad bridges toward Glendive.

articles.headline: Republican County Convention.
articles.text:
Pursuant to a call issued by J. C. Fisher, chairman of the county central committee, a convention of the Republican voters of Billings county was held at Medora on Saturday evening, August 16, for the purpose of appointing two delegates to the territorial convention to be held at Pierre on September 17, to nominate a delegate to congress.

After calling the convention to order and reading the call as published Mr. J. C. Fisher was elected chairman and L. H. Palmer secretary.

On motion of John Warn a committee consisting of the chairman of the convention and four others named by the chair, viz., John Warn, G. D. Kennedy, T. J. Kerr and W. F. Houk, were appointed to choose delegates. The committee after a short consultation reported the names of F. H. Ertel, of Belfield, and A. T. Packard, of Medora, as the delegates to represent Billings county at the territorial convention.

After a neat and appropriate address by F. H. Ertel and one of John Warn's characteristic speeches the first political convention of Billings county adjourned amid general good feeling and entire unanimity.
articles.summary: Report of Billings county's first Republican convention, which chose F. H. Ertel and A. T. Packard as delegates to the territorial convention at Pierre.

Wise & Goodkind, Bismarck, Dak. — wholesale dealers in wines, liquors, cigars, case & bar goods.
articles.summary: Directory of display advertisements on page 4 (standing ads, including Packard's insurance agency, Medora lots and the N. P. Ref. Car Co. beef cattle sale).

articles.summary: Directory of cattle- and horse-brand advertisements in columns 5-7 of page 4 (same standing brand ads as the previous issue; right edge cut by binding).

events.date_basis: Black Hills trip letter refers to "a July sun"; trip made in July 1884 (exact day not given)
events.title: Cow Boy party visits Bear Gulch tin and gold mines in the Black Hills
events.summary: Packard's Black Hills party visited the Bear Gulch camp and Nigger Hill mining property west of Spearfish, dined with Mr. St. John and toured Mr. Chapman's tin claims, descending a shaft that held a snow drift.
events.excerpt: we found Mr. Chapman busily at work on one. An assay of his dump averaged 6 per cent. tin

events.date_basis: no date given; issue of Thu 21 Aug 1884
events.title: Cow Boy backs L. N. Cary as Billings county's legislative candidate
events.summary: The paper said Billings county had settled on L. N. Cary as its standard bearer ahead of the district legislative convention, due in a few weeks, and urged his election.
events.excerpt: The citizens of Billings county may indeed be proud of having decided upon such a man as L. N. Cary as their standard bearer.

events.date_basis: standing notice; no date of loss given; issue of Thu 21 Aug 1884
events.title: Gregor Lang advertises reward for strayed horses
events.summary: Gregor Lang of Medora offered $50 for the return of three young mares branded with a double or reverse P and a light sorrel pony.
events.excerpt: One bay mare, one brown mare and one roan mare, all young and branded double or reverse P on left shoulder

events.date_basis: notice says stolen "May [26?]"; day uncertain in scan
events.title: Team of gray horses stolen from A. Anderson at Belfield
events.summary: A. Anderson offered $125 for the return of a team of large gray half-Norman horses stolen from Belfield, Billings county, in May.
events.excerpt: the team of large gray horses, half Norman breed, weighing twelve and thirteen hundred pounds, stolen from Belfield

events.date_basis: no date given; clipped item in issue of Thu 21 Aug 1884
events.title: Texas fever reported among range cattle near Spearfish
events.summary: A clipped item reported Texas fever among range cattle near Spearfish, D. T., brought in by rail from Texas to Ogallala and driven north.
events.excerpt: It is said that Texas fever has appeared among some range cattle near Spearfish, D. T.

events.date_basis: "last Sunday" before Thu 21 Aug 1884
events.title: Station agent C. L. Brinker spends Sunday in Belfield
events.summary: Medora station agent C. L. Brinker spent Sunday in Belfield.
events.excerpt: C. L. Brinker, station agent, spent last Sunday in Belfield.

events.date_basis: "last week" before Thu 21 Aug 1884
events.title: Gill Kennedy makes a two-day visit to Belfield
events.summary: Gill Kennedy went down to Belfield for a two days' visit.
events.excerpt: Gill Kennedy was down to Belfield on a two days' visit last week.

events.date_basis: issue of Thu 21 Aug 1884, "this week"
events.title: Cow Boy issue delayed a day by train delays
events.summary: Because trains were delayed (after the washouts), the Cow Boy came out one day late.
events.excerpt: Owing to the delay of trains the Cow Boy comes out one day late this week.

events.date_basis: "to-morrow, Friday" after Thu 21 Aug 1884
events.title: J. C. Fisher and A. T. Packard to start for Deadwood
events.summary: J. C. Fisher and editor A. T. Packard planned to leave for Deadwood on Friday morning.
events.excerpt: J. C. Fisher and A. T. Packard start for Deadwood to-morrow, Friday, morning.

events.date_basis: "for the last few days" before Thu 21 Aug 1884
events.title: Stock inspector T. A. Matthews visits Medora
events.summary: T. A. Matthews, stock inspector for Dakota and eastern Montana, spent several days in Medora.
events.excerpt: T. A. Matthews, stock inspector for Dakota and eastern Montana, has been in the city for the last few days.

events.date_basis: "last Sunday" before Thu 21 Aug 1884
events.title: Six stock trains from Mingusville pass through Medora
events.summary: Six trains of stock shipped from Mingusville passed through Medora bound east.
events.excerpt: Six trains of stock past through here on last Sunday en route east.

events.date_basis: "last Saturday" before Thu 21 Aug 1884
events.title: Governor Pierce welcomed at Bismarck
events.summary: The Cow Boy reported Governor Pierce's arrival in Bismarck, where Judge Francis gave the welcome address to over 2,000 people.
events.excerpt: Governor Pierce arrived in the capital city on last Saturday and was given a hearty welcome by the Bismarckians.

events.date_basis: "last Friday" before Thu 21 Aug 1884
events.title: Eastern party bound for Yellowstone stops over to see the Bad Lands
events.summary: A large party from the east en route to the National Park stopped over at Medora to view the Bad Lands scenery and were well pleased.
events.excerpt: remained over on last Friday to view the wonderful and wierd scenery of the Bad Lands.

events.date_basis: planned after Capt. Wrenshaw returns from the washout; issue of Thu 21 Aug 1884
events.title: Improvements planned for Medora freight house
events.summary: Capt. Wrenshaw was to order the freight house partitioned into three rooms, with a platform, a large derrick and freight skids, once he returned from the washout.
events.excerpt: The west end will be partitioned off into three rooms, and a platform will be built on the same end.

events.date_basis: "since our last issue" (Thu 14 Aug 1884) to Thu 21 Aug 1884
events.title: Medora Stage and Forwarding Co. wins exclusive rail rates and buys coaches at Helena
events.summary: The stage company secured exclusive passenger and express rates to Medora from the railroad's Fee and Footner, while Barr and Deffebach bought all the coaches and some horses at Helena.
events.excerpt: Word has ceen received from Messrs. Barr and Deffebach that all the coaches and a number of the horses have been bought at Helena

events.date_basis: progress reported "since our last issue", Thu 14-21 Aug 1884
events.title: Stage stations, wells and road work under way on Medora-Deadwood line
events.summary: Four stage stations had been built with hay put up, wells dug and springs found, boulders cleared from the trail on Rocky ridge and the road-bed graded; A. T. Packard would be general manager, Rassie Deffebach superintendent of stages and J. C. Fisher local manager.
events.excerpt: Four stations have now been built and hay put up near these and several others.

events.date_basis: "the afternoon of August 18" (Monday) stated in text
events.title: Severe rain, wind and hail storm strikes Medora
events.summary: A storm that made up five miles northwest of town struck Medora with enormous rain, terrific wind and hail that broke every south window pane in some houses; no loss of life was known.
events.excerpt: One of the most severe rain, wind and hail storms within the memory of the traditional "oldest inhabitant" visited Medora on the afternoon of August 18.

events.date_basis: during the storm of August 18
events.title: Storm turns vacant "Cowboy saloon" building completely around
events.summary: The wind turned the unoccupied building north of the track known as the "Cowboy saloon" completely around, confusing two men returning from gathering wild plums; the billiard hall was also severely tested.
events.excerpt: The building on the north side of the track known as "Cowboy saloon," but now unoccupied, was turned completely around

events.date_basis: storm of Mon 18 Aug 1884; westbound train held "three days"
events.title: Storm washouts destroy five N.P. bridges between Medora and Glendive
events.summary: Five railroad bridges between Medora and Glendive were washed away, more than twenty-five miles of track damaged and telegraph lines cut; Monday's westbound passenger train was held at Medora three days.
events.excerpt: Five bridges between Medora and Glendive were washed away and more than twenty-five miles of track badly damaged.

events.date_basis: "Saturday evening, August 16" stated in text
events.title: Billings county holds its first Republican convention at Medora
events.summary: Billings county Republicans met at Medora with J. C. Fisher as chairman and L. H. Palmer as secretary, and named F. H. Ertel of Belfield and A. T. Packard of Medora delegates to the territorial convention.
events.excerpt: the first political convention of Billings county adjourned amid general good feeling and entire unanimity.

events.date_basis: "at Pierre on September 17" stated in text
events.title: Territorial Republican convention at Pierre to nominate delegate to Congress
events.summary: Billings county's delegates, F. H. Ertel and A. T. Packard, were to attend the territorial convention at Pierre to nominate a delegate to Congress.
events.excerpt: the territorial convention to be held at Pierre on September 17, to nominate a delegate to congress.

events.date_basis: hearing date "21st day of August, 1884" stated in notice
events.title: Land office hearing set on John Weber's homestead contest
events.summary: The Bismarck land office summoned the parties in John Weber's contest of a Billings county homestead entry, alleged abandoned, to a hearing on August 21.
events.excerpt: the said parties are hereby summoned to appear at this office on the 21st day of August, 1884, at 10 o'clock A. M.
